summary.text: Sir Isaac Newton was an English polymath and a key figure in the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment that followed.
His 1687 book Principia formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation, which formed the dominant scientific viewpoint for centuries until relativity superseded it.
He showed that the motion of objects on Earth and of celestial bodies could be accounted for by the same principles.

items.prompt: A stone falls to the ground and a planet circles the Sun. What did Newton demonstrate about the two?

options.label: The heavens follow perfect circles, unlike the Earth
The same principles can account for both
Earth's laws fail once objects leave the planet
Only planets, not stones, obey his laws of motion

items.explain: Newton demonstrated that the motion of objects on Earth and of celestial bodies could be accounted for by the same principles.

items.prompt: An engineer uses Newton's laws for a slow crane. Relativity replaced them as the dominant view, so is that a mistake?

options.label: Yes, because they fail at every speed
Yes, because they apply only to planets
No, because relativity has since been disproved
No, they remain good approximations at low speeds and weak gravity

items.explain: His laws still serve as sufficient approximations for physical phenomena involving low speeds and weak gravitational fields.

items.prompt: Newton and Leibniz share credit for infinitesimal calculus. How do their efforts compare?

options.label: They share credit, but Newton developed his years before Leibniz
They share credit, but Leibniz developed his years before Newton
Newton alone gets the credit for it
They built it together in joint work

items.explain: Newton shares credit with Leibniz for formulating infinitesimal calculus, although he developed calculus years before Leibniz.

items.prompt: Newton passed a beam of white light through a prism. What was the observation behind his theory of colour?

options.label: The prism paints colour onto white light
Colour comes only from the eye of the observer
The prism separates white light into the spectrum's colours
White light splits into heat and light

items.explain: He developed his theory of colour from the observation that a prism separates white light into the colours of the visible spectrum.

items.prompt: How did Newton spend the last three decades of his life?

options.label: Teaching at Cambridge until his death
In London, running the Royal Mint and improving coinage
Farming at Woolsthorpe, his boyhood home
As a Church of England bishop after taking holy orders

items.explain: He spent them in London as Warden and then Master of the Royal Mint, increasing the accuracy and security of British coinage. He refused holy orders.

items.prompt: A hot mug sits on a desk and slowly loses its warmth. Newton is credited with what first about such heat loss?

options.label: The laws of thermodynamics and the idea of entropy
An empirical law, the first heat transfer formulation
A theory that heat is a fluid flowing between bodies
The design of the first working steam engine pump

items.explain: Newton formulated an empirical law of cooling, which was the first heat transfer formulation.

paragraphs.heading: Who Newton was
paragraphs.text: Isaac Newton was an English thinker of many talents who lived from 1643 to 1727. He was a mathematician, physicist and astronomer, but also an alchemist, a theologian, a historian and an inventor. He stands as a central figure of the Scientific Revolution and of the Enlightenment that came after it. His work is seen as the most influential of all in bringing about modern science.

paragraphs.heading: One set of laws for everything
paragraphs.text: In 1687 Newton first published his Principia, short for Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy. The book established classical mechanics and achieved the first great unification in physics. In it he set out his laws of motion and of universal gravitation, and he showed that objects on Earth and bodies in the sky obey the very same principles. His laws stayed the leading scientific view for centuries, until the theory of relativity replaced them. They still work well enough whenever speeds are far below the speed of light and gravity is weak.

paragraphs.heading: Gravity explains the sky
paragraphs.text: Using his mathematical account of gravity, Newton derived Kepler's laws of how planets move. He also explained the tides, the paths of comets and the precession of the equinoxes, and this removed doubt that the planets circle the Sun. He reasoned that Earth is an oblate spheroid. Later measurements of Earth's shape by Maupertuis, Clairaut, La Condamine and others confirmed this, and that convinced most European scientists that his mechanics beat the older systems.

paragraphs.heading: Light, colour and calculus
paragraphs.text: Newton built the first reflecting telescope. He also developed a detailed theory of colour, starting from the fact that a prism splits white light into the colours of the visible spectrum, and gathered his work on light in the book Opticks in 1704. In 1665 he found the generalised binomial theorem and started on the mathematics that later became calculus. He shares the credit for calculus with the German mathematician Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, though Newton worked it out years before him.

paragraphs.heading: Early life
paragraphs.text: Newton was born at Woolsthorpe Manor, in a Lincolnshire hamlet, on Christmas Day 1642 by the calendar England used then. His father, also called Isaac, had died three months earlier. He arrived early and was so tiny that his mother said he could have fitted in a quart mug. When he was three she remarried and moved in with her new husband, leaving the boy with his grandmother. In June 1661 he entered Trinity College, Cambridge.

paragraphs.heading: Mint, Parliament and the Royal Society
paragraphs.text: At 26 Newton became the second Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge. He twice sat briefly in Parliament for the university. Queen Anne knighted him in 1705, and he spent his last thirty years in London running the Royal Mint, where he made British coins more accurate and more secure. He led the Royal Society from 1703 to 1727, died at 84, and became the first scientist buried in Westminster Abbey.
